n: Structural Causes of Abnormal Uterine Bleeding

faq.a: Yes, submucosal fibroids even <2 cm can disrupt the endometrial surface and cause significant bleeding.
faq.q: Can a small fibroid cause heavy bleeding?

faq.a: When equipment is available it is safe; otherwise hormonal therapy can control bleeding until referral.
faq.q: Is hysteroscopic polypectomy safe in low‑resource settings?

faq.a: NSAIDs can worsen renal function and increase bleeding risk; use tranexamic acid or hormonal agents instead.
faq.q: Why avoid NSAIDs in a patient with renal disease?

exam: A 38‑year‑old woman presents with 2‑week history of heavy menses and a 10‑week enlarged uterus. What is your next diagnostic step and why? — TVUS to differentiate fibroid from adenomyosis; size guides management.

A 52‑year‑old post‑menopausal woman has spotting. TVUS shows endometrial thickness 6 mm. What does this result mean and what should you do? — Thickness >5 mm warrants endometrial sampling to exclude carcinoma.

You have a patient with severe anaemia (Hb 7 g/dL) from fibroid bleeding but no blood products. What immediate measures can you take? — Give tranexamic acid, iron, and arrange urgent referral for surgical control.
How does a submucosal fibroid differ from an intramural fibroid in terms of bleeding risk? — Submucosal protrudes into cavity, directly irritates endometrium, causing heavier bleeding.
Why is hormonal therapy not the first choice for a large (>8 cm) fibroid causing bulk symptoms? — It does not reduce size; surgery or embolisation is needed for symptom relief.

A patient on tranexamic acid develops a new deep‑vein thrombosis. What is the pharmacologic rationale for stopping the drug? — Tranexamic acid reduces fibrinolysis, increasing clot stability; it can precipitate thrombosis.
What red‑flag feature would change your management from outpatient to urgent referral in a woman with AUB? — Post‑menopausal bleeding or rapidly enlarging uterine mass suggests malignancy.
Explain why endometrial sampling may be falsely negative in focal carcinoma. — A focal lesion can be missed if the pipelle does not reach the area; hysteroscopy improves detection.

ai.subject: Pathology
ai.summary: Structural lesions of the uterus are a major cause of abnormal uterine bleeding (AUB). Recognising the typical presentations, using limited imaging, and managing the underlying lesion are essential, especially in low‑resource settings.

b: PALM acronym (Polyps, Adenomyosis, Leiomyoma, Malignancy) categorises structural AUB.
Diagnosis is clinical plus targeted imaging; histology confirms malignancy.
sections.p: Structural causes refer to any anatomic lesion of the uterus that disrupts normal endometrial shedding, including polyps, adenomyosis, leiomyoma, and malignancy.

b: Mild: PBAC <100, no anaemia.
Moderate: PBAC 100‑200, Hb 10‑11 g/dL.
Severe: PBAC >200, Hb <10 g/dL or hemodynamic compromise.
sections.p: Severity is graded by blood loss (PBAC score), impact on daily life, and presence of anaemia.

b: Leiomyoma (fibroids) – especially submucosal.
Endometrial polyps – often post‑menopausal.
Adenomyosis – diffuse uterine enlargement.
Endometrial carcinoma – risk ↑ with obesity, nulliparity.
sections.p: In East African hospitals the most common structural lesions are leiomyoma and endometrial polyps; adenomyosis and malignancy are less frequent but critical to consider.

b: Fibroids: irregular enlarged uterus, may cause pressure symptoms.
Polyps: focal bleeding, often with normal uterine size.
Adenomyosis: uniformly enlarged, tender uterus.
Malignancy: post‑menopausal bleeding, weight loss.
sections.p: Patients report heavy or prolonged menstrual bleeding, intermenstrual spotting, or post‑coital bleeding. Palpable uterine enlargement suggests fibroids or adenomyosis.
Use the most available tools first; when a test is unavailable, rely on clinical clues and refer if possible.

t.b: Detects fibroids, polyps, adenomyosis; assesses endometrial thickness.
Rules out hyperplasia or carcinoma in women >45 y or with risk factors.
Direct visualisation and removal of polyps or submucosal fibroids.

b: Severe anaemia (Hb <8 g/dL) with hemodynamic instability.
Rapidly enlarging uterine mass.
Post‑menopausal bleeding.
Suspicion of malignancy on imaging or sampling.
sections.p: Identify features that demand urgent referral or intervention.

b: Fibroids: Myomectomy or uterine artery embolisation where feasible; otherwise tranexamic acid for bleeding control.
Polyps: Hysteroscopic polypectomy; if not possible, consider hormonal therapy to reduce bleeding.
Adenomyosis: Levonorgestrel‑IUS (if available) or NSAIDs; surgery only for refractory cases.
Carcinoma: Referral for staging and oncologic surgery; avoid hormonal agents.
sections.p: Treat the underlying lesion first; provide supportive care for blood loss.

b: Repeat TVUS at 6‑month intervals for fibroids >5 cm.
Screen for anaemia every 3 months until stable.
Encourage weight control and contraceptive use to lower endometrial cancer risk.
sections.p: Monitor menstrual pattern, haemoglobin, and uterine size; counsel on risk factors.

b: Coagulopathy – prolonged bleeding despite normal imaging.
Ovulatory dysfunction – irregular cycles, no anatomic lesion.
Endometrial (primary) – dysfunctional shedding without structural change.
sections.p: Distinguish structural AUB from non‑structural (COEIN) causes.

b: TVUS may miss small polyps (<5 mm).
Endometrial thickness <4 mm does not exclude carcinoma in post‑menopausal women with bleeding.
CBC may underestimate chronic blood loss if iron stores are high.
sections.p: Be aware of limitations of bedside tools.

whenToSeekHelp: Severe anaemia with dizziness or tachycardia
Signs of infection after invasive procedures
